user.title: Before you install
user.description:
**This is alpha software and there are no guarantees that it runs.** It is shared with the Home Assistant community for testing and feedback, and no guarantees are given on data integrity or on consistency of functionality at this time.

**It restores state to devices that act in the physical world.** The default mirrored domains include `climate`, `water_heater`, `vacuum` and `timer` — so a stale or wrong restore can change your heating setpoint or hot water, not just a value on a dashboard. `alarm_control_panel`, `person` and `device_tracker` are **opt-in and off by default**; if you turn them on, an alarm's state is mirrored too.

Provided as is, without warranty and without liability. Prove a failover on a system you do not depend on, before you depend on one.

fileset.title: Config replication
fileset.description:
Everything `configuration.yaml` includes is replicated automatically — `configs/`, `themes/`, `packages/` and so on are followed, so you do not list them here.

This is for what no parser can see: files an integration opens by path at runtime. Anything found in your config directory is offered below; you can also type a path.

choose.title: How does this node reach Valkey?
choose.description:
**Direct** is what almost everyone wants: one Valkey or Redis server, reached by host and port.

**Sentinel** is for a Redis Sentinel cluster that elects its own primary. The code path exists but is **deferred and untested** — choose it only if you already run Sentinel and are willing to be the first to prove it.

transfer.title: Copying the bundle onto this host
transfer.description:
The bundle was written **inside** Home Assistant's container. It has to reach `/etc/cluster-sync` on the host this container runs on.

Leave all three blank if you are already at a terminal on that host.

🚨 This is about **this** node only. Nine of these files carry this node's identity — installing them on the other node would make it claim this one's id, and both would then believe they lead. The other node runs its own wizard.

None of these answers is saved.

data.host: Host address (blank if you are on it already)
data.user: SSH username (blank for your current one)
data.key_path: SSH key path (blank for your default, or if you use a password)

domains.title: What crosses to the standby
domains.description:
Which entity domains are mirrored and restored on the node that takes over.

The defaults are conservative on purpose: stateful things a promoted node needs to know, and nothing whose restore could actuate hardware.

**Adding `light` or `switch` is a real decision.** Restoring one writes a state change, and a state change is what automations trigger on — so a restored value can fire an automation and turn real things on. Check what triggers on them before adding them.

`person`, `device_tracker` and `alarm_control_panel` also tell anyone who can read the shared store when the house is empty. Pair them with TLS and a dedicated user.

data.include_entities: Individual entities to mirror as well (optional)

data_description.include_domains: Leave empty to use the built-in defaults.
data_description.include_entities: Full entity IDs, for one-off entities in a domain you do not want wholesale. They need not exist yet.

container.title: This node's runtime and radios
container.description:
**`docker` — the default, and right for most installs.** The promoter runs `docker start` / `docker stop` on one container. Fast, needs no project file, and nothing else in your estate can break it.

**`compose` — when nobody starts the container by hand.** Home Assistant is one service in a compose project, possibly behind a profile. The promoter acts on that service alone (`up -d --no-deps`), never the whole estate, and stops it with `stop` — never `down`, which would remove the container a demoted node needs in order to be promoted again.

🚨 **Compose mode needs an env file.** Compose interpolates the *entire* project file before it filters by profile or service, so one unset variable in a service you are not touching aborts the command. The promoter runs from systemd with none of your shell environment — without an env file it fails at exactly the moment it is needed.

**Radio liveness.** The promotion probe asks Home Assistant whether it is alive, and Home Assistant can be alive while every radio behind it is dead — that happened here, with a Zigbee daemon livelocked for 32 minutes while its healthcheck said `healthy`. Naming entities that update on reception makes the silence visible. It does **not** trigger failover: promoting because a radio died would move your house to a node whose radios may be no better.

data.compose_profile: Profile (if the service is behind one)
data.compose_env_file: Env file to source before every compose call
data.radio_watch: Entities that prove a radio is receiving

data_description.compose_file: Full path on the host, e.g. /srv/docker/compose.yml
data_description.compose_service: The service name in the file, not the container name.
data_description.compose_profile: Leave empty if you do not use profiles.
data_description.compose_env_file: Strongly recommended. Sourced and exported before compose runs.
data_description.radio_watch: Globs, e.g. sensor.*_rssi_numeric. Creates a 'radio silence' sensor showing seconds since any of them was last heard from. ⚠ Watch ONE radio's signals — the sensor reports the FRESHEST match, so mixing a Wi-Fi RSSI in with your Zigbee or RF sensors means the Wi-Fi masks the dead radio. Check the sensor's 'status' attribute, not just its value: 'no_reports' means the entities exist but no radio has ever been heard from, and that reads as unknown rather than a big number. Leave empty to skip.

history.title: Your history, and where it lives
history.description:
Home Assistant keeps a **history database** — the record of what happened and when: that you switched the kitchen light on at 19:04 last Tuesday, that an automation ran, that the temperature fell overnight. It is what every graph and the logbook are drawn from.

Each machine normally keeps its **own** copy, so if the other one takes over, its graphs start blank from the day it was built.

**Shared database** — both machines write to one PostgreSQL or MariaDB. Nothing to copy, history is simply continuous, and it works with either standby model. See Home Assistant's own guide: {recorder_docs}

**Dedicated database** — each machine keeps its own SQLite file. Simpler, nothing extra to run. History can still follow a failover, but **only with cold standby**: swapping the file requires Home Assistant to be stopped, so a warm node cannot do it without a restart — which would make it slower than cold.

data.history_database: Where does the history database live?

data_description.history_matters: Say no if you only care that the house keeps working and do not mind a gap in the graphs.
data_description.history_database: This choice decides which standby models you are offered on the next screen.

statistics.title: History that survives a failover
statistics.description:
Only **long-term statistics** cross between nodes — the years of energy and climate data behind the Energy dashboard and long-range graphs. On this kind of estate that is about half a megabyte a day.

Recent raw history — the logbook, the last ten days of detail — does **not** cross. It churns roughly sixty times faster, and replicating it was measured at 4 GB a day. After a failover your long graphs are intact and the logbook starts fresh.

**One manual step.** Years of existing statistics cannot arrive half a megabyte at a time, so the standby needs a one-off seed file that you copy across yourself (on an estate this size, about 500 MB — a few seconds over a wired network). Once this is set up, press **Write statistics seed** on the Cluster page and follow the instructions it gives you.

This uses the same encryption key as the config replication, so leave that switched on.

data.statistics_window_days: How far back each update reaches

data_description.statistics_window_days: Also how long the standby may be switched off and still catch up completely. 30 days costs about 4.5 MB per update; 90 days about 12.5 MB.
data_description.statistics_interval_minutes: How much history a failover can lose. Home Assistant compiles statistics every five minutes, so anything faster than that republishes the same data.

error.unsafe_shell_value: One of these values contains a character that cannot be used here — most likely a quote, a space, a backtick, or one of ; & | $ ( ). These values are written into scripts this host runs as root, so anything that could change what those scripts do is refused. Check the container name, config path, Valkey host, username and peer address.

abort.reconfigure_successful: Cluster State Sync reconfigured. The host bundle has been regenerated — reinstall it on this host if any host-side value changed.

fileset_degraded.title: Standby config fileset is degraded
fileset_degraded.description: The host-side swap could not put a fresh copy of the config fileset in place before this instance started (reason: {reason}). Decision D4 promotes anyway rather than refuse to boot, so Home Assistant is running, but integrations, devices, and the mobile app's login may be missing or out of date. Check the swap log on the host, and reload this integration once a fresh fileset has been staged and swapped in.

statistics_schema_mismatch.title: Standby cannot store history: recorder schema mismatch
statistics_schema_mismatch.description: The standby refused the replicated long-term statistics because its recorder schema is a different version from this node's ({detail}). It refuses rather than guessing, because writing rows shaped for one schema into another corrupts history in a way that opens cleanly and is wrong. Its history has stopped advancing and will have a hole from now until this is fixed. Bring both nodes to the same Home Assistant version, then start the standby's Home Assistant once so its recorder migrates.

statistics_gap.title: Standby's history has a gap that will not close
statistics_gap.description: The standby has been out of contact for longer than the statistics window reaches back, so the history in between is on neither node and no later window will contain it ({detail}). Everything from here forward will replicate normally. To recover the missing stretch, widen the statistics window and wait one publish, or write a fresh seed and copy it across.

statistics_not_seeded.title: Standby has no history to replicate into
statistics_not_seeded.description: Long-term statistics are being published, but the standby has nowhere to put them ({detail}). Years of statistics cannot arrive through the window — it carries about half a megabyte a day — so the standby needs a one-off seed. Use the 'Write statistics seed' button, copy the file it names to the same path on the standby, and the next pull there will adopt it automatically.

statistics_stalled.title: Standby's history replication has gone quiet
statistics_stalled.description:
The standby has not reported applying long-term statistics for several publish intervals ({detail})

This alarm exists because silence used to be indistinguishable from success: the standby's status expires, the warnings clear themselves, and replication that had stopped looked exactly like replication that was working.

flush_snapshot.description: Write this node's entity state to the shared store now. Refuses on a node that does not hold cluster leadership.
